items.title: nomos-analysis: FactIdentity, FactReader, FactStore and invalidation
items.why: The load-bearing architectural bet, still untested. FactIdentity is the cache key AND the identity, one type, so a fact cannot be reused under a key that does not describe it. items.done_when: A change in any one of FactIdentity's components invalidates, asserted component by component rather than in aggregate. Require() returns the honest degraded Applicability on failure and never a fabricated fact. Reading through FactReader records an edge; a test proves a read that recorded no edge is not possible.

items.title: Which of several usable offers wins
items.why: Registry::Resolve picks the first usable offer in provider-name order. items.title: Nothing walks the selection the floor bought
items.why: P8-SELECTION made Selection::Weaker reachable and nothing spends it. A caller lowers its floor to Approximate because a parser refuses seven files, the registry hands back the parser and the scanner in order, and Slice::Dispatch asks the parser and degrades the run on refusal — so the coverage the floor admitted is available and unused. The prior question is not the dispatch loop: a FactKey names the provider that answered, so per-subject fallback files one capability's facts under two providers within one run. Whether that is a coherent store or two answers to one question under one address is a decision, and it has to be reached before the loop is written.
items.done_when: The decision is recorded first, against a stated criterion. Then either the run walks the selection per subject — with the store still single-valued for what a file declares at a given generation, and RunReport naming which provider answered for how many subjects — or a record states why per-subject fallback is refused and what a caller should do instead. A negative control confirmed red either way: with fallback, a run where the strong provider refuses must not report the corpus clean.

items.title: The markdown round trip D-129 decided and nobody built
items.why: D-129 is a governing record, accepted, in the store, and it says markdown remains the surface people author through via a round trip that reads a record out as markdown and writes the edit back, as a transaction against the store: claim, stage, preview, commit, with the preview mandatory. None of that exists. Nothing reads a record out and nothing writes one back. Amended at version 2 to say so, which makes the gap schedulable and does not close it. What follows is the part that matters: records under docs/records are still the substrate in practice — authored as files, seeded into the store from those files by include_str!, edited as files — so the store holds a copy and the direction of that dependency is the opposite of what D-129 decides.
items.done_when: A record can be read out of the store as markdown byte-identical to what would be seeded from it, and an edit to that markdown can be written back as a transaction that previews what it changes before committing. Identity survives the round trip: the node_id, the blocks and the relations are the same afterwards, and a rename is an ordinary edit. The preview names whether normative wording moved, because D-129 calls that mandatory and a preview that cannot say it is not the preview the record decided. Either docs/records stops being the authoring substrate, or a record states why it remains one and D-129 is amended again to agree with the tree.

items.title: An item's verification is weaker than the gate it stands in for
items.why: work finish runs the item's argv and records the item done if it exits zero. Every item's argv is a cargo test invocation. The gate in .github/workflows/gate.yml is clippy with -D warnings and then cargo test, and the workspace denies unwrap_used, indexing_slicing and arithmetic_side_effects — a panic on the analysis path is a determinism defect rather than a bug, which is why they deny. So an item can be recorded verified while the gate that follows it is red. That is not hypothetical: P9-SKIP and P9-PHASE-GAP were both recorded verified with a clippy error in a file the item had just written, caught by running clippy by hand afterwards. Twice in three items, by somebody being careful — which is the arrangement the ledger exists to stop relying on, and the same sentence OD-LEDGER-001 already had to write once.
items.done_when: An item cannot be finished by a predicate that checks less than the gate does. Either finish refuses an argv that does not cover the gate, or the ledger derives the predicate rather than taking it from the author, or a record states why a weaker predicate is right and what the author is expected to run instead. Whichever is chosen, the two instances above would have failed under it, and a test says so.

items.title: work list calls an item ready when nothing can claim it
items.why: This item was authored on a false premise and is rewritten rather than deleted, because the premise is the interesting part. It said depends_on is unenforced. Whoever takes this must not add a second enforcement: two guards for one rule is how they come to disagree.

items.title: Every item claims docs/records, so the ledger runs one item at a time
items.why: All eight open items on this ledger reserve docs/records. Not most - all of them, measured. So exactly one item can be held at a time, whatever else the ledger says about parallelism, and nomos-ledger opens by stating that territory-based exclusion exists "so that several agents can work one repository without silently overwriting each other". On an audit ledger every item names a suspected defect, so the rule that was written to stop territory being under-declared now guarantees that every item excludes every other one. Two agents cannot work this repository concurrently by construction, and the mechanism reports that as a queue rather than as a design limit.

items.title: Abandoning an item destroys more of the record than crashing does
items.why: Measured against the code rather than the commit message that noticed it. nomos work abandon requires --reason and the ledger drops it. ReleaseOutcome::Abandoned carries reason: String non-optionally, which is the same technique the doc comment on ReleaseOutcome praises for the finished arm - carrying the evidence in the signature so that a release cannot express itself without one. The store then destructures it away: in Release, the Finished arm writes verified = Some(record) and the Abandoned arm is a `{ .. }` pattern that sets state = Ready and nothing else. Adjacent arms of one match, one persisting its evidence and one discarding it. The claim goes to None, the item goes back to Ready, and afterwards nothing on the item says it was ever held. The one reason this ledger does persist belongs to ItemState::Declined, where the doc comment says it is carried in the variant so an item cannot be declined reasonlessly - and it survives because it is part of the state rather than part of the transition. That is the structural line: a reason attached to a state is kept, a reason attached to a transition is not, and only one of the two is enforced at the type level. The consequence inverts the crate own stated intent. item.rs says a lapsed claim does not release itself, and stays visible so that a person can see the work was abandoned rather than never started. So an agent that dies holding a claim leaves a visible record, and an agent that abandons deliberately, having been made to write down why, leaves none. The well-behaved path is the lossy one. Observed on 2026-08-09 releasing P9-ONE-DIRECTION: the reason given said where the work had got to and why it stopped, and it survives only in the message of commit a749f9a, which is the half-recorded shape OD-SPEC-005 and commit 20296d9 both exist to name.
items.done_when: An abandonment is readable from the ledger after the fact. The reason the holder gave, who gave it, and when, survive on the item that was abandoned, and are reachable through the surface that reports an item rather than only by reading the file. A test asserts this over a claim-then-abandon cycle. The negative control is confirmed red: the test must fail when the abandoned arm goes back to discarding the reason, which means asserting the stored text itself and not merely that a field is present. A second control holds the line the crate already draws - abandoning must still return the item to Ready and still clear the claim, because a record of an abandonment must not go on excluding anyone. Whether a lapsed claim is owed the same treatment, which the crate deliberately leaves visible and for which nobody writes a reason, is settled either way in the record rather than left open.

items.title: A loud predicate is recorded as no verdict, because nothing drains its pipe
items.why: StdProcessLauncher pipes a predicate stdout and stderr and reads neither until after the child has exited. The wait loop calls try_wait, sleeps, and never drains. A child that writes past the pipe buffer blocks on the write, never exits, and is killed at the timeout, so a predicate that passed is recorded as no verdict at all. Demonstrated on a scratch ledger on 2026-08-09, same program and same 60 second timeout, only the volume changed: 840,000 bytes emitted in one second timed out after 60 seconds, and 4,000 bytes emitted the same way verified in zero. Met for real while finishing P10-FIRST-CHECK, whose predicate is cargo test --workspace: 75,751 bytes of output, 103 seconds by hand, TimedOut twice at 600 seconds under work finish. Every earlier item on this ledger scoped its predicate to one or two crates and stayed under the buffer, which is why four phases of work never met this. The consequence is the one shape this repository keeps recording. P9-PREDICATE separated GateFailed from PredicateFailed because a failing gate and failing work are different facts, and NoVerdict was added so that nobody found out could not read as bad work. This defect turns the failure direction into a lie in the other direction: a run that did find out, and found nothing wrong, is written down as nobody found out. Worse for a failing run, where the failure detail is exactly what makes the output large: the louder the failure, the more likely it is reported as a timeout rather than as a failure.
items.done_when: A predicate that writes more than the pipe buffer is verified on its result rather than killed on its volume. The check is a test in nomos-platform-std that runs a program emitting several hundred kilobytes quickly under a short timeout and asserts ExitOutcome::Exited with the real code, which fails against todays launcher. Both negative controls hold: a program that genuinely exceeds its timeout must still report TimedOut, and the captured output must still be the program actual output rather than a truncated prefix that happens to fit. Whether the fix drains on threads, uses a growing buffer, or moves to a platform crate that already solves it is open. Once it lands, P10-FIRST-CHECK predicate can drop the -q it carries only to fit the buffer, and the ledger recorded evidence for that item stops being a run of empty doctest sections.

items.title: Two guards disagree about whether DECLARED_RULES is mirrored
items.why:
nomos check and the contract test table give different answers to the same question about the same universe, and one of the two is a false claim of coverage. mirror.rs judges a declared universe by the mirror it names at the site, in its doc comment, and resolves that name against real parsed test functions. DECLARED_RULES in crates/spec/nomos-spec-validate/src/run.rs names none, so nomos check reports it as an admitted gap: declares no mirror, Advisory. The UNIVERSES table in tests/contract/tests/completeness_universes.rs classifies that same constant as Standing::Mirrored by Test_A_Rule_Nobody_Declared_Should_Fail_The_Run. The arithmetic isolates the disagreement exactly. Sixteen declared universes; the table calls four mirrored and twelve unmirrored, with UNMIRRORED_TOTAL at 12; nomos check finds thirteen unmirrored; the single difference between the two sets is DECLARED_RULES. The module documentation at the top of mirror.rs says thirteen, twice, so the rule and its own prose already disagree with the table.
The table is the one that is wrong, and it is worth saying why rather than which. Test_A_Rule_Nobody_Declared_Should_Fail_The_Run builds a synthetic Fake carrying the invented id NSV-INVENTED-001 and asserts that Validate reports it undeclared. It exercises the reconciliation mechanism against input the test made up. It never compares DECLARED_RULES against the rules this crate actually implements, and nothing else does either. Registered() in preserve.rs is a second hand-written list of the same four rules, and Validate reconciles the two hand-written lists against one another, which is precisely what makes the pair look covered: two lists agreeing catch a disagreement between two hands, never a divergence from the code. A fifth impl Rule added to preserve.rs and left out of Registered() is absent from both lists, is never run, and is reported by nothing. That it is invisible even to the scanner is a second fact: Read_Universes does not recognize a function returning Vec<Box<dyn Rule>> as a universe at all, so the list that enumerates the real thing is not judged by the rule that judges lists.
The severity ordering mirror.rs sets for itself is what makes this an item rather than a footnote. A phantom mirror is Blocking and an admitted gap is only Advisory, because a false claim of coverage is worse than a hole somebody wrote down and counted. This claim escapes that ordering only by being written in a hand-maintained table in another file, where the rule that judges coverage claims cannot resolve it. The three instances OD-COMPLETENESS-001 analyses were each repaired by naming the mirror at the site, which is why nomos check reports none of them; DECLARED_RULES is the one row the table calls mirrored that did not follow that convention. Noticed while finishing P10-FIRST-CHECK and recorded until now only in the Consequences section of D-134, which is the half-recorded shape OD-SPEC-005 exists to name.
items.done_when: The two guards agree about DECLARED_RULES, and the agreement is checked rather than asserted once by hand. Either DECLARED_RULES gets a real mirror - a check comparing it against the rules the crate actually implements rather than against a second hand-written list, named at the site so that nomos check resolves it - or the table admits the gap and UNMIRRORED_TOTAL rises to thirteen. Which of the two is the decision this item makes, and the record says why rather than only which. A test then fails when the workspace scan and the classified table disagree, over the whole universe set and not for this one constant, so that the next divergence is caught rather than recounted by hand. That test must name the universe it disagrees about and not merely compare two totals, because two totals that happen to match conceal which row moved. The negative control is confirmed red by restoring the classification the table carries today and watching it fail with DECLARED_RULES named. There is no such pair. Five open items reserve a record; every one of them also reserves crates/spec/nomos-spec-store or a parent of it, and every one of them also reserves tests/contract.
This is not an accident of who authored what. OD-LEDGER-001 third authoring rule requires that anything writing a canonical record also reserve crates/spec/nomos-spec-store, because such a record must be seeded in governing.rs with the literal count in governing_records_are_present.rs raised or the workspace goes red. Two items writing two different records must therefore both edit the same two files. They cannot be independent, by construction, and the rule that makes it so was added in the same work as the guarantee it defeats. P10-RECORD-LOCK set out to end exactly this: before it, all nine open items reserved docs/records and the second claim was always refused. Reserving the record instead of the directory removed one edge and left the deeper one in place.
OD-LEDGER-004 already measured it without drawing the conclusion. It lists twenty-two pairs still excluded on genuine code overlap, naming crates/spec and crates/spec/nomos-spec-store at six blocked pairs and tests/contract at five, and treats them as ordinary code contention. What it does not say is that for record-writing items specifically the store overlap is guaranteed by its own authoring rule, so the acceptance test passed at the time only because some pair on the board happened to be disjoint for unrelated reasons. The property was measured true once and is not structurally maintained.
A second global serializer arrived later and independently. P9-PUBLIC-API checks each crate public surface into tests/contract/surface, so any item widening any crate API must update a file under tests/contract, and items are now being widened to reserve that whole directory for the same reason they reserve the store. Two items updating two different snapshot files collide on the directory that holds them, which is the shape P10-RECORD-LOCK named for records, one level up and not yet applied here.
Observed on 2026-08-09. The last concurrent pair existed at 340a310 and went at 91f8159, a widening commit, which by design takes no claim and runs no predicate. No open item predicate builds nomos-ledger except P10-ABANDON-REASON, which is how a red test in nomos-ledger survived several commits with nobody informed - the same shape as a check in a crate the predicate never builds, which is the omission two widening commits on this board have already corrected for themselves.

Either two items writing different records can be claimed at once for a structural reason, or the property records_do_not_serialize asserts is restated to one that can actually hold, and which of those it is gets recorded with the reason rather than left to whoever next reads a red suite. items.why: Measured on 2026-08-09 rather than inferred. LedgerItem derives Deserialize with no deny_unknown_fields and no schema version, so a nomos.exe built before a field existed reads the current work/ledger.json, ignores the keys it does not know, and writes the document back without them. No error, exit 0. The state change survives and the dropped data does not, so a lossy write is indistinguishable from a successful one at the surface that reports it. The evidence. e88f92d added LedgerItem::abandoned as a Vec<Abandonment> with serde(default) and no skip_serializing_if, so a current binary always emits an empty abandoned list on every item. A round trip through the current binary against a scratch ledger under NOMOS_WORK_DIR confirms that directly: work claim wrote the key to all fifty items and work abandon persisted the reason text verbatim. The repository ledger holds zero such keys. An abandonment of P10-ABANDON-REASON written at unix 1786326402 through a freshly built binary was gone by 1786326839, when another session's work claim rewrote the file - the release stood, the reason did not. This did not start today. Both e88f92d and 6326566 committed a work/ledger.json with zero abandoned keys, including the very commit that added the field, so the authoring session was stripping it as it wrote it and nothing said so. What produced it is the documented Windows workaround rather than carelessness. work finish cannot run under cargo run, because the predicate rebuilds the exe that is the running process, so sessions copy target/debug/nomos.exe and run the copy - and a copy taken before a schema change is a stale writer for the rest of that session. The workaround for a file lock became a silent data loss channel on a file two sessions share. The shape is OD-LEDGER-006 one level down. That record is about a reason attached to a transition not surviving it; this is a reason attached to an item not surviving the next writer, and it fails the same way, by looking like success. The reason destroyed here is worth keeping, because it is the first thing the new field was ever asked to hold: the work was complete and committed at e88f92d, the item's predicate runs -p nomos-ledger which is red on records_do_not_serialize for a cause outside the item, that cause is on the board as P10-SEEDING-SERIALIZES, and the claim reserved the two paths every open item also reserves, so it was refusing the one item able to fix the reason it could not finish.
items.done_when: A write by a binary that does not understand the document it is writing either fails or preserves what it did not understand. Which of those is settled in the record on stated grounds rather than left to whoever implements it: a schema version the writer must recognise, deny_unknown_fields on the way in, or a preserved passthrough of unknown keys. A test asserts it over a document carrying a key the deserializing type does not declare, and asserts on the round tripped document rather than on whether a type compiles. The negative control is confirmed red - removing the guard must fail that test and fail it alone. A second control holds the line the crate already draws: a writer that does understand the document must still round trip it unchanged, because a guard that refuses every write is not a fix and would stop the board rather than protect it. Whether the copied binary workaround is replaced, or only documented so an operator can tell a stale writer from a current one, is settled either way, since a guard that reports only after the loss leaves the operator holding the same problem.

items.title: A lapsed lease invalidates the whole ledger, so one dead agent stops every claim
items.why: Measured on a scratch ledger under NOMOS_WORK_DIR rather than inferred from reading. Document validation in store.rs treats state Claimed with no active claim as a violation - X is marked claimed but has no active claim. A lease expiring is precisely that state, so the moment any lease runs out the whole document stops validating. FileLedger::Claim loads the document before it does anything else and the load validates, so every claim then fails, not only a claim on the lapsed item. Reproduced by forcing one lease into the past and then claiming P9-AUTHORING, which shares no territory with the lapsed item: refused. Meanwhile work list still reports P9-AUTHORING as ready, so the board goes on advertising work nobody can take - the defect P9-DEPENDS-ON closed, reappearing through a different cause. The report also names the wrong thing. Claim writes self.Load().map_err of a closure discarding its argument into ClaimRefusal::NoSuchItem at store.rs:518, so every load failure - an invalid document, an unreadable file, a parse error - is reported as no item named X. The operator is told the identifier is wrong when the ledger is broken. That is why this needed an experiment rather than a glance, and it is a reason attached to a failure not surviving it, the same shape as OD-LEDGER-006 for the third time. Recovery exists, but only for the holder. Renew and Release match on the holder and do not take the validating path, so the agent holding the lapsed claim can renew or abandon it and the board recovers at once. Anyone else is refused: abandoning as another holder is refused with overlaps territory held by dead-agent until unix 1000000000, a lease twenty-five years expired and still excluding. So when the holder is a process that died - which is the only reason a lease ever lapses on its own - nothing on the board can be claimed, renewed or abandoned by anybody, and the only recovery is editing work/ledger.json by hand. MAXIMUM_LEASE exists so that a crashed agent does not hold territory until somebody edits the file, and item.rs says exactly that at the definition of the lapse check. The lease expiring is what causes the thing the lease exists to prevent. The unit level being right is what hid it: Has_Active_Claim returns false on a lapsed claim and its tests pass, and validation refuses the document before exclusion is ever consulted, so the correct answer never gets to matter. This is live rather than theoretical - a four-hour lease was outstanding on this board while it was written.
items.done_when: A lapse behaves the way MAXIMUM_LEASE was introduced to make it behave: an agent that dies holding a claim stops excluding everybody else, and the board keeps working without a human editing the file. What a lapsed claim leaves visible on the item is settled in the record rather than assumed - the crate has already decided a lapse should be distinguishable from work never started, and that decision is not reopened here. A test claims an item, forces its lease into the past, and asserts three things: an unrelated item is still claimable, validate does not call the document invalid, and the lapsed item itself is either claimable or explicitly is not on stated grounds. The negative control is confirmed red and confirmed alone - restoring the violation must fail those tests and nothing else, since a control that reddens the whole suite proves nothing about what it guards. Separately, a load failure names its cause: Claim stops mapping every load error to NoSuchItem, and a test asserts that an invalid document and a genuinely missing item produce different messages, asserting the text itself because the defect is precisely that two causes wore one name.

D-132 puts the corpus above the plan, so this is the strongest form the package question has, and neither id appears anywhere in this repository: not in docs/records, not in work/ledger.json, not in source.

PackageKind in crates/contracts/nomos-contracts/src/package.rs enumerates sixteen kinds and matches the volume's package_kind list variant for variant, LanguagePackage and RulePackage among them. It has zero consumers outside nomos-contracts. Cargo.toml line 70 sets publish = false for the whole workspace. Every crate inherits it through publish.workspace = true and carries a hand-written uniform version = "0.1.0". Its final revised layout is a flat crates/ holding nomos-checks and nomos-gates, with providers/ as a top-level sibling. So the directory layout is not the finding and is not what this item is about. The versioning property is, and it is measurable at HEAD.

items.title: The guarantee that a judging command cannot report success vacuously is one command remembering, not a type refusing
items.why:
nomos check cannot report a clean run over nothing. An empty walk exits ExitCode::Vacuous, 6, and says so, and the doc comment names the sibling defect it exists against: check-standards-tree /nonexistent walked nothing, found nothing and reported CLEAN. That guard is real, it is tested, and it is better than what it replaces.

It is also entirely local. The enum lives in crates/host/nomos-cli/src/check.rs and is private to that group's module; spec.rs declares its own 6 as Absent. Nothing in nomos-contracts makes a success value unconstructible without evidence that something was judged, so no type stops the next judging group from returning Ok over an empty subject set. The guarantee is one command remembering.

check.rs argues the placement, and argues it well: the guard belongs in the caller "because did I see a plausible amount of the world is a question only the caller that chose the tree can answer". That is a real argument and it is in a doc comment. A cross-command guarantee decided in one module's prose is a decision the next author does not encounter, because the next author reads their own module.

OD-LEDGER-002 already records that nomos-gates, nomos-findings and nomos-applicability do not exist. It does not record how the guarantee those crates were meant to carry is held in their absence. That is the gap here: not the missing crates, which are on the record, but the missing statement of what replaced them and where it now lives.

OD-GATE-001 is this same defect one level out - a skipped test reports ok - and it is closed. This workspace has already decided once that it will not rely on a command remembering to be honest about having run nothing.
items.done_when: Where the no-vacuous-success guarantee lives is decided and recorded rather than argued in a doc comment. Either caller-side placement stands, and the record states what makes the next judging command inherit the guard instead of remembering it - a shared entry point every group routes through, a contract test over every group that can print a verdict, or an explicit acceptance that it is per-command with the cost named and a place it will be noticed. Or the guarantee moves into a value that a judging command cannot construct without having judged something, and the record says what that costs at the seam and what it does not cover. Building nomos-gates is not required to close this, and neither is adding a second judging command: the question is where the property is held, and it can be answered while there is still only one.

items.title: A documented flag makes an item permanently unclaimable and stops every other claim, non-retryably
items.why: work add advertises --territory-pattern in its usage and README documents it beside --territory. Any item carrying one entry in territory.patterns makes Territory::Intersect return Unknown against every other territory - crates/substrate/nomos-ledger/src/territory.rs:130 short-circuits on patterns before comparing a single path - so Refusal_From maps it to UnknownIndependence, whose Is_Retryable is false. The consequences are worse than an item nobody can claim. That item can never be claimed by anyone, its own holder included; every other claim on the board is refused against it; and the refusal tells an agent the independence question is unanswerable, which by the exit-code contract in README means stop and fetch a human rather than try another item. Nothing in work add warns, and validate accepts the document, so a single documented flag bricks the board for every session at once and the failure does not look like contention. Refusing an unanswerable overlap rather than granting it is correct and is the README rule; what is wrong is that the only way to reach that state is an advertised flag for a feature the comparison does not implement. This was found by reading territory.rs while measuring the boards serialization, not by an incident - no open item uses a pattern today, which is why the cost of closing it now is a test and a refusal.
items.done_when: A territory pattern either compares or is refused where it is authored, and it is no longer possible to reach UnknownIndependence through a documented flag. If patterns are refused, work add rejects --territory-pattern with a message naming what is unsupported, the flag leaves the usage text and README, and the refusal is a usage error rather than a ledger error so it cannot be mistaken for contention. If patterns compare, Territory::Intersect answers Disjoint or Overlaps for a pattern against a path and Unknown is reserved for a question the mechanism genuinely cannot answer. Which of the two is the decision this item makes and the record says why, since refusing a flag the README documents is a narrowing of what the ledger offers and OD-LEDGER-001 is the standing statement of what territory promises. A test claims against an item carrying a pattern and pins the outcome, and the negative control is that restoring the unconditional Unknown at territory.rs:130 turns it red. items.title: The three verbs that change the board read and write it without taking the lock the doc comment says they take
items.why: With_Lock at crates/substrate/nomos-ledger/src/store.rs:228 acquires the cross-process lock and its doc comment says every mutation goes through it. Claim, Renew and Release do not. That is a read-modify-write over a whole-document file, so two sessions interleaving lose one of the two writes entirely, and what is lost is not a field but every change the other session made to any item. The failure is silent and looks like the ledger simply not having recorded something. It is close in shape to the loss P10-STALE-WRITER is open for, and is a different cause with the same symptom, which is why it wants separating rather than folding in: a stale binary drops fields it does not know, and this drops changes it never read. Found while designing P10-STALE-WRITER, in territory that item does not need.

items.title: Blessing one crates surface rewrites every crates surface, so a concurrent worker loses its own
items.why: tests/contract/tests/public_surface.rs:15 says the variable rewrites every snapshot, and it does. That is harmless for one author working alone and wrong for this tree, which is worked by several agent sessions at once by design and says so in README. Observed on 2026-08-09 between two live claims: the holder of P10-FACT-BYPASS blessed to update tests/contract/surface/nomos-rules.txt, which rewrote the three snapshots the holder of P10-SPEC-DETERMINISM had deliberately changed and not yet committed; that holder reverted the three foreign files, and the other holder found its own work silently reverted mid-lease and re-applied it by hand. Both behaved correctly and the data survived because a human-shaped agent noticed. Nothing in the mechanism noticed. The failure mode is worse than it looks: blessing rewrites a snapshot to whatever the current tree exports, so a foreign snapshot carrying an uncommitted change is not merely reverted to HEAD but rewritten from a half-finished tree, and the result still passes the surface test. It is territory violation by a tool rather than by an author, and territory cannot express it because the writer is a test the other worker also has to run.
items.done_when: Blessing writes only the snapshots the blesser asked for. The variable names what to rewrite - a crate, or a list of them - and naming nothing rewrites nothing rather than rewriting everything, so the widest possible action is not the easiest one to reach for. The deliberate failure after a bless stays, because a bless that passes is a check anybody can switch off, and that reasoning is unchanged. A test asserts that blessing one crate leaves another crates snapshot byte-identical, including when that other snapshot disagrees with the tree - which is the case that actually bit, and the negative control is that restoring the rewrite-everything behaviour turns it red. The doc comment at the top of the file stops saying every snapshot. No new record: OD-GATE-002 already states what the surface check is for and this does not change it.

items.title: Four package kinds carry a suffix the corpus taxonomy does not, and the label is what a peer reimplements
items.why: Found by P10-PACKAGE-SEAM and recorded in OD-PACKAGE-001 rather than fixed, because renaming a protocol surface was outside a versioning items done_when. The game plan carries three copies of the package taxonomy and they disagree: two match volume 03s sixteen kinds exactly, the third omits RepositoryProvider and suffixes four names. items.why: Found by P10-MIRROR-DISAGREEMENTs eighth negative control and measured, not inferred: renaming a universes claimed mirror to a name that resolves to nothing produced [Advisory] ... resolves to no check ... and the check index is incomplete, because 1 subject(s) could not be read, and nomos check exited 0. items.title: A projection that agrees with its own stamp is not thereby what the store renders
items.why: Check compares two things and not the third. It rebuilds the projection, compares the recorded inputs_digest and profile_digest against the rebuild, and compares the body on disk against the stamp own content_digest. It never compares the body against rebuilt.body, which Build has already produced and which is sitting in the same function. So an edit to the body that also updates content_digest to match reports "is current" and exits 0. Measured on 2026-08-09 by appending a line to diagrams/relations.mmd and rewriting content_digest to the new hash: exit 0, no finding. The existing negative control, Test_A_Rewritten_Stamp_Should_Not_Excuse_The_File_It_Describes, rewrites the digest to a bogus value, so it proves the comparison reads the sidecar rather than trusting it and never probes the consistent case. This matters more now that a projection is committed and gated: P10-REQUIRED-PROJECTIONS makes CI assert that a shipped output is derivable from the store, and what it actually asserts is that the output agrees with a stamp beside it, which the same commit can rewrite.

Check compares the rendered bytes it already holds, and the difference between "the store moved" and "somebody typed into the file" survives the change rather than collapsing into one verdict. A test appends to a rendered body, rewrites content_digest to the appended body own hash, and asserts the comparison still refuses it. The freshness command reports the new case in its own words rather than reusing the edited sentence, if the two are distinguishable at the seam.

items.title: One crate chooses the platform, runs the verb and renders the answer, and a second adapter would duplicate all three
items.why:
The README plans transports around a headless core, with the CLI as one adapter and IPC, gRPC and MCP as others. nomos-cli is the only place any of them could be written from today. It is 4104 lines across six modules: spec.rs 1509, work.rs 1047, check.rs 827. work.rs imports FileLock, StdFileSystem, StdProcessLauncher and SystemClock from nomos-platform-std directly, so choosing a platform, running a verb and rendering its outcome are one body of code with no seam between them.

Naming a concrete provider here is not the defect. OD-RULES-001 makes nomos check a composition root deliberately, and a composition root is exactly the place permitted to name concrete things. The defect is that nothing separates composition from orchestration: a second adapter wanting the same work verbs would have to re-derive the claim, lease and finish sequence rather than call it, and the two copies would then drift with nothing able to notice.

This is cheapest to settle while there is one adapter and no second caller to migrate. It gets more expensive with every command added, and the board has more commands queued than it has adapters.
items.done_when: Where application orchestration lives is decided and recorded. Either a seam exists between choosing a platform, running a verb and rendering its outcome, such that a second adapter can call the middle one without taking the other two, and the work group is the case that demonstrates it. Or the record states why one crate holding all three is right for as long as there is one adapter, names what that costs, and says what would make it wrong. Not closed by moving code into modules inside nomos-cli: a module boundary no second crate can depend on is the same coupling at a different indentation.

README line 36 calls nomos-contracts protocol truth that depends on serde and nothing else. Cargo.toml line 3 calls it the only authoritative statement of Nomos semantics. AGENTS.md says that when two authorities disagree the mechanical one wins and the disagreement is a defect worth an item. Here the mechanical one is also the narrow one, and the wide claim sits in a workspace manifest comment that nothing reads back.

What is actually missing is an admission rule rather than a phrase. Test_Contracts_Should_Depend_On_The_Allowlist_And_Nothing_Else constrains what band 0 may depend on, and Test_The_Readme_Should_List_Every_Member_At_Its_Declared_Band constrains where a member is listed. Nothing constrains what may be added to nomos-contracts, so the criterion is whatever the comment says, and every concept in the product can argue that it is a statement of Nomos semantics. The crate holds ten modules today and the argument for the eleventh is already written for it.

Nothing in the crate is wrong yet, which is the reason to settle it now rather than after a finding, an architecture delta or an agent type has been admitted on the strength of a sentence nobody chose.

The criterion says what earns admission rather than listing what has been admitted so far: crossing a subsystem, process or plugin boundary and needing one stable shared representation is the candidate, and the record says what a domain-local concept does instead. items.title: Six normative requirements govern the work ledger, none is cited, and the blocker taxonomy drops one of their seven causes
items.why:
Volume 12 of the v14 corpus carries six normative requirements, WORK-LEDGER-001 through WORK-LEDGER-006, at authority canonical-normative-record and maturity accepted, in section volume-12.10-4-2-work-ledger-verification-and-decomposition. They govern the work ledger. Not one of the six identifiers appears in any tracked file in this repository: not in docs/records, not in work/ledger.json, not in source, not in a test. Measured by resolving all 363 requirement ids under 01_authoring/artifacts/requirements against every file git ls-files reports.

That alone would only say the corpus is large and this build is young. What makes it an item is that the ledger demonstrably descends from these requirements and diverges from four of them without anywhere to read why.

WORK-LEDGER-005 names seven typed blocker causes: dependency, decision, territory mismatch, external resource, needs-split, stale probe artifact, and other. Blocker in crates/substrate/nomos-ledger/src/item.rs enumerates six of them, in that order, with matching semantics and near-matching wording. StaleProbeArtifact is the one that is absent, and the string "stale probe" appears nowhere in the tree. Six of seven in the corpus order is not convergent evolution; it is derivation with one variant dropped, and because no id is cited nobody can tell whether it was declined or overlooked.

WORK-LEDGER-001 lists thirteen things an item shall be addressable by. LedgerItem carries twelve of them - id, title, why, done_when, territory, state, depends_on, blocked, claim, verification, verified, and abandoned covering recorded completion evidence. The missing one is priority, and "priority" appears nowhere in nomos-ledger or nomos-cli. This board is worked by picking an item off a list that has no ordering, which is the cost, and it is currently paid without having been priced.

WORK-LEDGER-004 requires that verification recorded at completion time be distinguished from a later reverification sweep, and that a failed sweep create a visible regression record rather than erase the original evidence. LedgerItem::verified is a single Option<VerificationRecord>. There is no sweep, and a second write to that field would overwrite the first - the same class of loss OD-LEDGER-006 recorded for abandonment reasons and fixed there by making abandoned a list.

WORK-LEDGER-006 requires generated projections of the ledger by item, state, feature and testing status. Eighteen projection profiles exist and every one of them projects the specification store; none reads work/ledger.json.

WORK-LEDGER-002, four testing dimensions per feature with completion requiring each done or explicitly declined, has no counterpart in the schema at all. WORK-LEDGER-003, a predicate declared before work starts, is the one the tree already honours in substance, since finish keeps "no predicate at all" as its own answer.

P10-PACKAGE-SEAM is the precedent and the reason this is worth opening rather than noting. ARCH-001 and ARCH-002 were in exactly this position - corpus requirements about a subsystem this repository had already built - and D-132 puts the corpus above the plan. The answer there was two records that decided what the requirements bind and what they do not. This is the same question about the subsystem that has had more items spent on it than any other.
items.done_when:
Whether WORK-LEDGER-001 through WORK-LEDGER-006 bind this build is answered and recorded, in the shape OD-PACKAGE-001 and OD-PACKAGE-002 used for ARCH-001 and ARCH-002: each of the six accepted, deferred with what the deferral costs, or read as not reaching this build with the reason a corpus requirement does not bind the thing built to enforce it. Blanket answers are refused - the six differ, and 003 is already satisfied while 002 has no counterpart, so one verdict covering all six would be a verdict about none of them.

The record states, for WORK-LEDGER-005 specifically, whether StaleProbeArtifact is a declined variant or a missing one, because six of seven in corpus order is the strongest evidence in this item and it is the cheapest thing here to get wrong. Blocker gains that answer at the site the way D-134 put a universe mirror next to it, so the next reader of the enum does not have to re-derive the comparison.

Not closed by adding fields. Any schema change this decision calls for is a follow-on item with its own territory, because the exhaustive undeclared-key probe lives in tests/exclusion_holds.rs, which three open items already reserve. This item ends at a decision that names what would have to become true.

items.title: A run cannot report that a subject needs an agent, so the seventh reporting category CHK-003 requires has no state to be reported in
items.why:
CHK-001 through CHK-007 are normative requirements in volume 05 governing what a check run reports. CHK-003 is the one this item is about: every run shall report evaluated, excluded, unsupported, unavailable, failed, not-applicable, and agent-required combinations.

Applicability in crates/contracts/nomos-contracts/src/applicability.rs answers six of those seven and does it well. Supported, SupportedWithFallback and PartiallySupported are evaluated; ConfigurationDisabled is excluded; MissingCapability is unsupported; ProviderUnavailable and DependencyUnavailable are unavailable, split because the remedy differs; AnalysisFailed and Unparseable are failed, split for the same reason; NotApplicable is not-applicable and its doc comment already calls it the only positive statement about the absence of a judgment.

There is no agent-required. Ten variants, and none of them says a subject needs a model to judge it.

That absence is load-bearing rather than cosmetic, because the concept is already in the tree one layer away. EvidenceClass in the same crate carries AgentJudged, documented as the floor a claim arrives at when nothing corroborates it, and EvidenceClass::Is_Mechanical exists precisely so a model judgment cannot be reported as a check having passed. So the protocol knows the difference between mechanical and agent-produced evidence when it describes a claim, and has no way to say it when it describes coverage.

The consequence is that a subject requiring an agent has nowhere honest to go. It gets filed as MissingCapability, which says no installed provider offers the capability and points the reader at installing something, or it is left out of Coverage entirely. Coverage in crates/kernel/nomos-model/src/evidence.rs counts evaluated and excluded and lists gaps, and Coverage::Debt filters gaps to those that are coverage debt rather than deliberate absences. Agent-required is neither: it is work that can be done, by something that is not a provider. Both available answers are wrong in the direction this type exists to prevent.

The enum head comment says the type is deliberately exhaustive and that a consumer match should break when the protocol grows a state, because a new way for analysis to be incomplete is exactly the kind of change a consumer must not silently absorb. Agent-required is a way for analysis to be incomplete, and it is being absorbed silently today by having no variant at all.

Related but not the same question as P10-VACUITY-HOME, which is about where the no-vacuous-success guarantee lives. This is about whether the vocabulary can express the case at all.
items.done_when:
Whether CHK-003 binds this build is answered, and if it does, a run can say that a subject requires an agent without that being indistinguishable from a missing provider or from silence.

If the requirement is accepted, Applicability gains the state, Coverage gains whatever bucket keeps it out of both evaluated and Debt, and the record says which of the two current mis-filings each was, so the change reads as a correction rather than an addition. A test asserts that an agent-required subject is neither reported as evaluated nor counted as coverage debt.

If it is deferred or read as not binding, the record states that with the reason, and Applicability carries the answer at the site, so the next reader comparing the enum to CHK-003 finds the decision instead of repeating this audit.

Growing the enum breaks every exhaustive match on it by design. Those breaks are the item, not an obstacle to it, and any that fall outside this territory are named in the record rather than widened into it.

items.title: Three hundred and sixty-three requirements govern this build and fourteen are cited, so a requirement that is met and one that is not read identically
items.why:
The v14 corpus carries 363 requirements in 61 families under 01_authoring/artifacts/requirements, at authority canonical-normative-record. Resolving every one of those ids against every file git ls-files reports finds 14 named in a governing record, the ledger, or crate source. Of those 14, the ARCH and PKG cluster is deliberate, put there by P10-PACKAGE-SEAM; the rest are incidental mentions in the ingest pipeline.

The reflex reading is that the corpus is far ahead of the build, most of it governs phases nobody has started, and a low number is expected. That reading is wrong in the direction that matters, and measuring it is what produced this item.

Where the build has reached a requirement, it tracks it closely. EvidenceClass carries exactly EVID-001 eight classes, Authoritative through HumanAsserted, and EVID-001 also forbids collapsing them into one confidence number, which the type does not do. FactVariant carries exactly CAP-002 five variants. CAP-003 requires provider selection to compare guarantees and not merely availability, and selection.rs compares Guarantee on every axis and documents that it is deliberately not a score. Three requirements met, precisely, and not one of the three is cited anywhere.

Where it diverges, it diverges by one element and says nothing. Blocker carries six of WORK-LEDGER-005 seven typed causes in corpus order and drops StaleProbeArtifact. LedgerItem carries twelve of WORK-LEDGER-001 thirteen fields and drops priority. Applicability carries six of CHK-003 seven reporting categories and drops agent-required.

That is the finding. Met and unmet are the same shape from outside: an identifier that appears nowhere, next to code that may or may not honour it. The only way anyone has told the difference is by hand, three times in this repository so far, and each time it cost a full audit to establish something a machine could have reported. Three of the six comparisons above came out met, which means the hand audit is not merely expensive but mostly negative - the worst ratio a manual check can have.

This repository already refuses this exact class of ignorance everywhere else. tests/contract asserts the README tables against the workspace in both directions. OD-COMPLETENESS-001 records that a completeness guard is only as complete as its universe. D-134 makes a universe declare its own mirror. The one universe with no guard is the corpus that governs the whole product.

The machinery is also already here and pointed elsewhere: a traceability-matrix projection profile exists in nomos-spec-project, and like all eighteen profiles it projects the specification store rather than relating the store to the build.
items.done_when:
How a corpus requirement is related to this build is decided and recorded, such that a requirement which is met, one which is deliberately not met, and one which nobody has looked at are three distinguishable states rather than one.

The record names the bearer of the relation and why it is there rather than somewhere else - a citation at the implementation site, a registry the contract tests read, or a projection relating the store to the workspace - and states what it costs to keep honest, because a traceability surface that goes stale is worse than none. It says what happens to the 349 requirements nobody has assessed, since a scheme that requires all of them answered before any of them is answered will not be adopted.

Not closed by citing requirement ids in comments. A comment is not a universe and nothing reads it, which is the failure OD-COMPLETENESS-001 already recorded one scale down. Whether the answer is mechanically checked is itself part of the decision, and if it is not, the record says why the corpus is the one authority in this tree exempt from a guard.

Building the mechanism is a follow-on item. This one ends at a decision with a named first requirement family to carry it, and P10-LEDGER-CORPUS and P10-AGENT-REQUIRED are the two already open that would be its first two entries.

items.title: The gate is red because a committed record was never rendered, and the diagram it names is in nobody territory
items.why:
The gate is red on dev right now, at the Required projections step, and has been since 401b2d0.

That commit registered OD-GATE-004 and did not re-render diagrams/relations.mmd. The diagram last moved in c42f93b, one commit earlier, so the committed body is missing every OD-GATE-004 edge - eleven of them, since the record relates to seven others and seven relate back. `nomos spec freshness --into . --require diagram-set` is gate.yml step 51 and fails on exactly this.

Nobody did anything wrong in a way a rule would have caught. P10-RERENDER-HAZARD wrote the obligation into AGENTS.md in ea3c167, which is after 401b2d0, so the commit that broke it predates the sentence telling authors not to. That is the ordinary way a hazard gets documented, and it leaves one artifact already broken behind it.

Two more commits have landed records since, including 840ec47 for OD-TRACE-001, so the delta is now larger than the one commit that started it.

What keeps this from being a one-command fix somebody does in passing is that the command cannot be run correctly by most sessions, for two separate reasons.

The first is stated in AGENTS.md: the store is built from the files on disk, so rendering beside another session unlanded record bakes their work into the output, and the gate then fails on the commit that carries it. At the time this item was written OD-LEDGER-012 and OD-SYNTAX-002 were both on disk uncommitted under live claims, which is the normal condition of this tree rather than an unusual one. A correct render needs a moment when every registered record is committed, or an isolated checkout that has only the committed ones.

The second is territory, and it is the reason this is an item rather than a note. diagrams/relations.mmd is in no item territory. Every item that adds a governing record reserves its own record paths and not the diagram, so an agent that correctly re-renders after adding a record is writing outside its claim, and an agent that respects its claim leaves the gate red. OD-LEDGER-001 records that territory is declared rather than enforced, so nothing stops the write - which means the current state is that the honest agents are the ones who leave it broken.
items.done_when:
diagrams/relations.mmd matches what the store renders, and `nomos spec freshness --into . --require diagram-set` exits 0 against a tree whose registered records are all committed.

The render is taken from a tree with no uncommitted registered record in it, and the item says which commit it was taken at, so a reader can tell a correct render from one that happened to be taken at a quiet moment.

The recurrence is addressed rather than only the instance, because this will happen again on the next record and the obligation in AGENTS.md is prose that a machine does not read. Either the diagram is reserved by whichever item adds a record - which means saying so where item territories get authored, since the guidance to reserve both record paths is in the nomos-spec-change skill and does not mention the diagram - or something derives the obligation the way the gate lint step is derived rather than restated. Which one is the decision, and if the answer is that authors must remember, the record says why a repository that derives its gate step from gate.yml is content to leave this one to memory.

Not closed by re-rendering and saying nothing. That is the instance, and the instance is the cheap half.

items.title: Which substrate is canonical for a feature request is undecided, and the typed layer encodes the answer
items.why: The typed FeatureRequest/DesignSpec/FeatureResult layer cannot be started until this is recorded, because the schema is the answer written down: authored files with typed front matter and a derived store index is a different schema from a store that is the durable substrate with docs/records rendered out of it. OD-SPEC-006 decided the question for governing records and left the alternative priced rather than refused - stop seeding from include_str, seed from the bundle, make docs/records rendered outputs with a freshness check, and design a guard, because OD-SPEC-005 refused the obvious one. OD-SPEC-007 has since paid part of that price in general form: it established that what makes the guard a check is that side B is authored independently of the directory it is compared against rather than that it is hand-typed in one file, and built registration files that keep the independence while removing the shared edit. So the price OD-SPEC-006 quoted is out of date in the buyers favour and nothing has restated it. Deciding this per artifact rather than once is the second-authority failure this repository is organised against: feature requests in one substrate and records in another would put the split in the schema of every typed row.
items.done_when: A record under docs/records with its own registration under crates/spec/nomos-spec-store/records decides which substrate is canonical for a feature request, on stated grounds rather than by preference, and restates the price of the alternative as OD-SPEC-007 left it rather than as OD-SPEC-006 quoted it. It says what the decision binds - the typed layer schema - and what it does not. Not closed by a record that says the question is open, and not by one that decides it for records again without saying what a feature request is.

abandoned.reason: Decided and drafted, not landed, and blocked by the tree rather than by the question. Landing a governing record adds relations, which leaves diagrams/relations.mmd stale and reddens the freshness gate step unless the commit re-renders; re-rendering now would bake OD-LEDGER-012 and OD-SYNTAX-002, two other sessions uncommitted records, into a committed file. Both halves of the AGENTS.md hazard cannot be satisfied at once right now, so the conservative half wins and no record is added. The freshness step is independently red already at exit 8 for the same missing render. The decision reached, on the evidence: a feature request is an authored file under docs/records with typed front matter and the store holds it as a derived index, not as the durable substrate. Three grounds. Nothing persists a specification database - corpus.rs still opens with that sentence and RECORDS in governing.rs is still a generated table of include_str over the record files, so what survives an invocation is the file. Deciding per artifact is the real hazard: files for records and the store for feature requests would put two substrates in one build and encode the split in every typed row, which is unreversible in a way the substrate choice itself is not. And the price OD-SPEC-006 quoted for the store is out of date in the buyers favour - OD-SPEC-007 paid the guard part by establishing that side B needs to be authored independently of the directory it is compared against rather than hand-typed in one file, so what remains is seeding from the bundle and making docs/records rendered outputs with a freshness check, neither of which is an open design question. Re-claim and land the draft once git status --porcelain over docs/records and crates/spec/nomos-spec-store/records is empty, then render diagram-set in the same commit.

items.title: A commit touching the ledger carries whatever other sessions wrote since the diff, and the message describes only its own item
items.why: work/ledger.json is one file and every session writes it, so git add work/ledger.json stages whatever other sessions added between the diff check and the commit. Nothing is corrupted and no territory rule is broken - territory governs who may write a path, and this is several sessions writing the same path legitimately - but commit messages systematically under-describe what they carry, and the history is the only place a reader can ask what a change was for. Verified twice inside five commits. 63d51ee asserts Nothing here is a code change; this commit is the transition, while its ledger diff adds P10-AGENT-REQUIRED and P10-CORPUS-TRACE, two items another session opened that the message never names. P10-CANONICITY-DECISION was itself introduced by bd724ee, whose subject is the P10-SYNTAX-V2 payload parser. 0b98305 is the counter-example proving this is avoidable rather than inherent: its subject is the opening of the item it carries.
items.done_when: A commit that changes work/ledger.json either describes the ledger transitions it carries, or cannot carry ones its author did not make. Which of those is the answer is the decision, recorded on stated grounds rather than settled by whichever is cheaper to write. If the answer is that authors must remember, the record says why a repository that derives its gate lint step from gate.yml rather than restating it is content to leave this one to memory - P10-DIAGRAM-OWED is being asked the same question about the diagram, and two answers that disagree must say why. Not closed by a hazard line in AGENTS.md unless the record exists and argues for exactly that. A mechanical answer - a verb that stages only the items its holder transitioned, or a check over the message - brings its own predicate and its own files, which means widening this territory before starting rather than during. The record is registered under crates/spec/nomos-spec-store/records or it is not governing.
